day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Clear customs, collect luggage, and take the Metro (Linha Vermelha/Red Line) from Aeroporto station to the city center for about €1.85. Check in to Lisbon City Stay and freshen up.
day_by_day.afternoon: After settling in, take a leisurely walk through the Baixa (Downtown) district. Stroll along Rua Augusta, pass through the iconic Arco da Rua Augusta (exterior is free to admire), and head down to Praça do Comércio overlooking the Tagus River. Soak in the atmosphere and get oriented with the city — all free.
day_by_day.evening: Explore the Alfama neighborhood at dusk. Walk up to the Miradouro das Portas do Sol viewpoint for a stunning free panoramic view of the city and river. Watch the sunset and enjoy the ambiance of Lisbon's oldest district.

meals.breakfast: Grab a coffee and pastel de nata (custard tart) at the airport or a nearby café upon arrival — budget around €2–3.
meals.lunch: Pick up a hearty bifana (pork sandwich) or prego roll from a local tasca near Baixa for €3–5.
meals.dinner: Dine at a traditional tasca in Alfama. Look for a menu do dia (daily set menu) with soup, main course, and dessert for €10–13. Try bacalhau à brás (salted cod with eggs and potatoes) as your introduction to Portuguese cuisine.

day_by_day.notes: Day 1 is intentionally light on activities given the 13:00 arrival. Use the afternoon and evening to orient yourself. Validate a rechargeable Viva Viagem card (€0.50) at the Metro for all public transport during the trip — much cheaper than single tickets.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — one of Lisbon's most unique and world-class museums housed in a stunning 16th-century convent. Admission is approximately €5 (reduced/free on Sunday mornings). Spend 2–3 hours exploring Portugal's extraordinary azulejo tile heritage, including a massive panoramic tile panel of pre-earthquake Lisbon.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Time Out Market Lisbon Food Tour experience in the Cais do Sodré area. Spend the afternoon sampling the best of Portuguese cuisine in one of Europe's most celebrated food halls — try petiscos (Portuguese tapas), fresh seafood, and local cheeses. Budget €15–20 for tastings across multiple stalls.
day_by_day.evening: Wander through the bohemian Bairro Alto neighborhood. Browse the streets, pop into local shops, and enjoy the vibrant pre-dinner atmosphere. Settle in for dinner at a local restaurant before the nightlife crowd arrives.

meals.breakfast: Start the day at a neighborhood pastelaria (pastry shop) near the hotel. Order a galão (milky espresso) and a tosta mista (toasted ham and cheese sandwich) for €3–4.
meals.lunch: Graze at the Time Out Market — budget €15–20 to sample 3–4 dishes from different vendors, including a glass of local wine.
meals.dinner: Find a budget-friendly restaurant in Bairro Alto offering a menu do dia or half-portions (meia dose) of classics like caldo verde soup and grilled sardines for €10–14.

day_by_day.notes: The National Tile Museum is closed on Mondays — Saturday is a perfect day to visit. From the museum, take bus 718 or a tram back toward the city center. Time Out Market is busiest on weekends, so arrive at the food hall before 13:30 to beat the lunch rush.

day_by_day.morning: Take the Belém Historical & Culinary Half-Day experience. Travel by tram 15E or bus 728 from the city center to Belém (about 20–30 minutes, €1.85). Visit the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a masterpiece of Manueline architecture — exterior is always free, interior entry is approximately €10. Then walk to the iconic Tower of Belém along the riverside (entry ~€6, or admire from outside to save money).
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue exploring Belém on your own after the guided portion. Visit the free Monument to the Discoveries (Padrão dos Descobrimentos) exterior and enjoy the riverside promenade. Stop at the famous Pastéis de Belém bakery — the original home of the pastel de nata since 1837 — for €1.20–1.50 per tart. Head back to the city center in the late afternoon.
day_by_day.evening: Explore the Mouraria neighborhood, Lisbon's oldest and most multicultural quarter, adjacent to Alfama. Visit the free Intendente square and enjoy a relaxed evening stroll through authentic local streets far from tourist crowds.

meals.breakfast: Enjoy a simple breakfast at the hotel or a nearby café — coffee and pastry for €2–3.
meals.lunch: Eat lunch in Belém at a local café or grab a bifana and a Sagres beer from a budget tasca near the monastery for €7–10.
meals.dinner: Try a tasca in Mouraria for an authentic, affordable dinner. Look for açorda (bread-based stew) or grilled fish with salad and house wine for €11–14.

day_by_day.notes: Many Lisbon museums offer free entry on Sunday mornings (before 14:00), including the Jerónimos Monastery interior — check current schedules closer to travel. Belém is about 6 km west of the city center; the tram 15E is scenic and budget-friendly. Wear comfortable shoes as Belém involves significant walking.

day_by_day.morning: Explore the historic Castelo de São Jorge (St. George's Castle) — one of Lisbon's most iconic landmarks perched atop the highest hill in the city. Entry is approximately €15 (look for discounts online or at the door). Enjoy sweeping views over the Alfama, Baixa, and the Tagus River. Spend 2 hours exploring the medieval battlements, towers, and the small archaeological museum inside.
day_by_day.afternoon: Descend from the castle into the Alfama district and spend the afternoon exploring its narrow labyrinthine streets, colorful tiles, and hidden squares. Visit the free exterior of the Sé de Lisboa (Lisbon Cathedral), one of the city's oldest buildings dating to 1147. Browse the local shops and street vendors for affordable souvenirs like ceramic tiles, cork products, and tinned fish.
day_by_day.evening: Head to Miradouro da Graça — one of Lisbon's lesser-known but most beautiful viewpoints — for a golden-hour panorama over the city. It's completely free and less crowded than the more touristy Miradouro de Santa Luzia. Afterward, enjoy a relaxed dinner in the Intendente or Anjos area.

meals.breakfast: Visit a local mercearia (grocery/deli) near the hotel and pick up fresh bread, local cheese, and fruit for a self-assembled budget breakfast under €4.
meals.lunch: Grab lunch at a tascas in Alfama — a simple prato do dia (plate of the day) with soup, bread, and a drink for €8–11.
meals.dinner: Dine in the up-and-coming Anjos neighborhood, where local restaurants cater to residents rather than tourists. A full dinner with wine should cost €10–13.

day_by_day.notes: Monday is when several major Lisbon museums are closed (including the National Tile Museum), so it's the ideal day to focus on outdoor sights like the castle, Alfama streets, and viewpoints. Wear very sturdy, non-slip shoes — Alfama's cobblestones are steep and uneven. Consider buying a bottle of water from a supermarket (€0.50) rather than cafés (€1.50+).

day_by_day.morning: Visit the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) — Portugal's most important art museum featuring works by Hieronymus Bosch, Albrecht Dürer, and Portuguese masters. Entry is approximately €6. Spend the morning immersed in Portuguese art history from the 12th to 19th centuries, including the famous Panels of São Vicente de Fora.
day_by_day.afternoon: Spend your final afternoon in the charming Chiado and Príncipe Real neighborhoods. Browse the independent bookshops and boutiques along Rua do Carmo, visit the free exterior of the ruined Igreja do Carmo (Gothic church destroyed in the 1755 earthquake — interior entry ~€5 if interested), and relax in the beautiful Jardim do Príncipe Real park. Pick up last-minute souvenirs at budget-friendly shops.
day_by_day.evening: End your Lisbon trip with a farewell dinner in Chiado or Baixa. Splurge slightly on a proper sit-down meal of bacalhau (salt cod prepared your way — there are said to be 365 recipes!), paired with a glass of Portuguese vinho verde. Finish with a final pastel de nata and a bica (espresso) at a classic Lisbon café.

meals.breakfast: Treat yourself to a proper sit-down breakfast at a traditional café in Chiado — coffee, fresh orange juice, and toast with butter and jam for €4–6.
meals.lunch: Pick up a sandwich, olives, and local cheese from a Chiado deli or supermarket for a picnic in Jardim do Príncipe Real — budget €5–7.
meals.dinner: Farewell dinner at a mid-range tasca in Chiado or Baixa. Budget €15–18 for a full meal with wine — a slight splurge to close out the trip on a high note.

day_by_day.notes: If your departure flight is on May 19 or 20, plan your final evening accordingly and allow extra time to get back to the airport. The Metro Red Line from Alameda or Oriente to the airport takes about 20–30 minutes and costs €1.85. Keep your Viva Viagem card loaded for the airport trip. Total estimated daily budget per person (excluding accommodation): €40–55/day covering transport, entry fees, and meals.

trip_options.title: Classic Lisbon, Portugal Experience
trip_options.description: The sweet spot between comfort and value. Enjoy quality accommodations, diverse experiences, and good food.

day_by_day.morning: Arrival at Lisbon Airport at 13:00 — no morning activities scheduled. Clear customs, collect luggage, and take the Aerobus or Metro (Red Line to Green Line) to your hotel, Lisbon City Stay. Journey takes approximately 30–40 minutes. Check in, freshen up, and orient yourself with a neighbourhood walk around the hotel area.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Time Out Market Lisbon (Mercado da Ribeira) for your first taste of Portuguese cuisine. Spend 2–3 hours exploring the iconic food hall, sampling dishes from top local chefs — try bacalhau à Brás, pastéis de nata, and a glass of vinho verde. This is a perfect low-key, self-paced introduction to the city's food scene after a long travel day.
day_by_day.evening: Stroll along the Ribeira waterfront (Cais do Sodré) and enjoy the early evening atmosphere. Head to the Bairro Alto neighbourhood for dinner at a traditional tasca. Recommended: Taberna da Rua das Flores — a beloved local spot serving seasonal Portuguese small plates at mid-range prices. End the night with a short walk back to the hotel.

meals.breakfast: On the plane or grab a quick coffee and pastel de nata at the airport upon arrival — A Padaria Portuguesa inside the airport is a solid local chain option.
meals.lunch: Time Out Market Lisbon — budget €12–18 per person sampling multiple stalls. Try the bifanas (pork sandwiches) and fresh seafood options.
meals.dinner: Taberna da Rua das Flores, Bairro Alto — traditional Portuguese small plates, approx. €25–35 per person including wine.

day_by_day.notes: Day 1 is intentionally relaxed given the 13:00 arrival. Avoid booking tours or timed entries today. Purchase a 24-hour Viva Viagem metro card (€0.50 card + top-up) at the airport to make transport easy. The Time Out Market is a 10-minute taxi or 20-minute metro ride from the airport, making it a convenient first stop.

day_by_day.morning: Start the day with breakfast near the hotel, then head to the Alfama District for the Alfama Walking Tour & Fado Show (morning portion). Explore Lisbon's oldest and most atmospheric neighbourhood with a guided tour through narrow medieval alleyways, past the Sé Cathedral, and up to the Miradouro da Graça viewpoint for panoramic city views. The tour typically runs 2–3 hours in the morning.
day_by_day.afternoon: After the walking tour, visit the Castelo de São Jorge (St. George's Castle), perched above Alfama. Wander the ramparts and towers for sweeping views of Lisbon and the Tagus River. Entry is approximately €15. Spend 1.5–2 hours exploring. Afterwards, descend back through Alfama's winding streets and stop for lunch at a local restaurant in the neighbourhood.
day_by_day.evening: Return to Alfama for the Fado Show component of the experience — most Fado houses begin performances around 20:00–21:00. Book a dinner-show at a mid-range Fado restaurant such as Clube de Fado or Mesa de Frades. Enjoy authentic Portuguese music in an intimate setting while dining on traditional dishes like arroz de pato (duck rice) or grilled fish.

meals.breakfast: Café near the hotel — look for a local pastelaria. Try a galão (milky espresso) with a tosta mista (toasted ham and cheese) for a classic Portuguese breakfast. Budget €4–6.
meals.lunch: A Tasca do Chico or similar local tasca in Alfama — hearty lunch specials (prato do dia) typically cost €10–14 including bread, drink, and dessert.
meals.dinner: Fado dinner show at Clube de Fado or Mesa de Frades — budget €40–55 per person including dinner and the show. Reservations strongly recommended, especially on weekends.

day_by_day.notes: Alfama's cobblestone streets are steep and uneven — wear comfortable walking shoes. Sunday can be quieter in some areas but Alfama remains lively. Book the Fado dinner show in advance as weekend slots fill up quickly. The Castelo de São Jorge is a short uphill walk or a quick Tuk-tuk ride from the Alfama tour starting point.

day_by_day.morning: Take Tram 15E or an Uber (approx. 20 minutes) out to Belém for the Belém Historical & Culinary Half-Day experience. Begin with a visit to the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery — one of the finest examples of Manueline architecture in the world. Explore the ornate cloisters and church. Pre-book tickets online (€10) to skip queues. Spend approximately 1.5 hours here.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue the Belém experience with a visit to the iconic Torre de Belém (Tower of Belém), a 16th-century fortress on the banks of the Tagus River — a must-see Lisbon landmark (€6 entry). Afterwards, indulge in the culinary highlight of Belém: visit the original Pastéis de Belém bakery (open since 1837) for the world-famous custard tarts, eaten warm with cinnamon and powdered sugar. Stroll along the waterfront promenade and visit the Monument to the Discoveries before heading back to the city centre.
day_by_day.afternoon_extra: Optional: Visit the MAAT (Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology) nearby if you have energy — striking modern architecture on the waterfront.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and explore the elegant Chiado neighbourhood. Browse independent bookshops and boutiques. For dinner, try a contemporary Portuguese restaurant in Chiado such as Alma or Cantinho do Avillez (José Avillez's casual bistro) — both offer elevated Portuguese cuisine at mid-range prices and showcase local ingredients.

meals.breakfast: Pastéis de Belém — arrive early (before the tour crowds) for fresh custard tarts and a bica (espresso). Budget €5–8. This is a quintessential Lisbon breakfast experience.
meals.lunch: Lunch at a local restaurant near Belém waterfront — try Restaurante Feitoria or a simpler option like Solar dos Presuntos for grilled fish or cataplana (seafood stew). Budget €15–22.
meals.dinner: Cantinho do Avillez in Chiado — modern Portuguese bistro, approx. €30–40 per person. Alternatively, Taberna Moderna for a slightly more casual setting at €20–30.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is approximately 6km west of central Lisbon. Tram 15E from Praça da Figueira is the scenic option but can be crowded. An Uber or taxi (€8–12) is more comfortable and reliable. Book Jerónimos Monastery tickets online in advance — queues can be very long in May. Belém fills up mid-morning, so aim to arrive by 09:30.

day_by_day.morning: Visit the National Tile Museum (Museu Nacional do Azulejo) — one of Lisbon's most unique and underrated museums, housed in a stunning 16th-century convent. Explore Portugal's 500-year tradition of decorative azulejo tile-making, from Moorish geometric patterns to elaborate Baroque panels. The museum's highlight is a 23-metre panoramic tile panel depicting pre-earthquake Lisbon (1755). Allow 2 hours. Entry is approximately €5.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Mercado de Campo de Ourique for the Local Neighbourhood Stroll experience. This beloved local market, away from tourist crowds, offers fresh produce, artisan cheeses, charcuterie, wine, and prepared foods. Explore the surrounding residential neighbourhood of Campo de Ourique — a charming, authentic area with independent cafés, bookshops, and local boutiques. This is a wonderful contrast to the more touristy zones and gives a real feel for everyday Lisbon life.
day_by_day.evening: Explore the vibrant Príncipe Real neighbourhood for the evening — known for its antique shops, garden square, and excellent restaurant scene. Visit the Jardim do Príncipe Real for a relaxing sunset moment. Dine at a neighbourhood restaurant such as O Corvo or Tasca Kome for a more intimate, locally-loved dining experience.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at a local café near the hotel or en route to the Tile Museum. Try Café de São Bento or any neighbourhood pastelaria — coffee and pastry for €4–6.
meals.lunch: Mercado de Campo de Ourique — graze on market stalls offering petiscos (Portuguese tapas), fresh bread, cheese, and charcuterie. Budget €12–18 for a satisfying market lunch with a glass of wine.
meals.dinner: O Corvo in Príncipe Real — intimate neighbourhood restaurant with excellent seasonal Portuguese cooking, approx. €25–35 per person. Reservations recommended.

day_by_day.notes: The National Tile Museum is located in the Xabregas area, slightly east of the city centre — a 15-minute Uber or taxi ride (€8–10) from most hotels. Tuesday is a good day to visit as it tends to be less crowded than weekends. Campo de Ourique market is liveliest on weekday afternoons. The neighbourhood stroll pairs beautifully with the market visit as the area is very walkable.

day_by_day.morning: Dedicate the final morning to exploring areas you may have missed or revisiting favourites. Consider a leisurely walk through the Baixa-Chiado district — Lisbon's elegant downtown, rebuilt after the 1755 earthquake in a striking grid layout. Visit the grand Praça do Comércio on the Tagus waterfront, the ornate Elevador de Santa Justa (iron lift with rooftop views, €5.30), and browse the Rua Augusta pedestrian street. Pop into the historic Livraria Bertrand (world's oldest operating bookshop, founded 1732) in Chiado for a browse.
day_by_day.afternoon: Head to the Miradouro do Parque Eduardo VII or the Parque das Nações (Expo area) for a relaxing final afternoon. Alternatively, visit the Museu Nacional de Arte Antiga (National Museum of Ancient Art) for a dose of Portuguese painting and decorative arts if history is calling. Do some last-minute souvenir shopping — look for azulejo tiles, ginjinha (cherry liqueur), Vinho Verde, Portuguese ceramics, or locally-made cork products at Conserveira de Lisboa or A Vida Portuguesa.
day_by_day.evening: Celebrate your final evening in Lisbon with a memorable dinner. Treat yourself to a slightly elevated experience at Taberna Sal Grosso or Zé da Mouraria — both offer outstanding traditional Portuguese food in a warm, authentic atmosphere at reasonable prices. After dinner, enjoy a final ginjinha at A Ginjinha in Rossio square (a beloved Lisbon institution since 1840, shots cost €1.40) and take a last evening stroll along the waterfront.

meals.breakfast: A proper sit-down breakfast at Café Nicola or Café Martinho da Arcada — two of Lisbon's most historic cafés on Praça do Comércio / Rossio. Try ovos mexidos (scrambled eggs) or a full breakfast spread. Budget €8–12.
meals.lunch: Light lunch at a cervejaria (beer hall/seafood restaurant) in Baixa — try Cervejaria Ramiro's more affordable cousin, Solar dos Presuntos, for grilled seafood and cold Super Bock beer. Budget €18–25.
meals.dinner: Taberna Sal Grosso or Zé da Mouraria — traditional Portuguese cuisine, approx. €25–35 per person with wine. Book ahead. End with ginjinha at A Ginjinha in Rossio (€1.40 per shot — a perfect, cheap Lisbon farewell ritual).

day_by_day.notes: If departing on Day 6, confirm your flight time and arrange airport transport the evening before. The Metro from Baixa-Chiado or Rossio to the airport (Red Line) takes about 35–40 minutes. Allow at least 2.5 hours before departure. A Vida Portuguesa (Chiado or Intendente) is the best single stop for high-quality, beautifully packaged Portuguese souvenirs at fair prices — highly recommended for last-day shopping.

meals.lunch: Upon settling in, head to Pharmácia Restaurant in Chiado — a chic, design-forward restaurant set inside a former pharmacy, offering refined Portuguese cuisine with stunning city views.
meals.dinner: Dinner included as part of the Fado Show experience at a premium Alfama Fado house such as Sr. Fado or Clube de Fado — expect traditional dishes like caldo verde, grilled fish, and local wines in a candlelit setting.

day_by_day.notes: Flight is TAP Air Portugal (TP). Allow 45–60 minutes for baggage claim and transfer. Pre-book a private luxury transfer from the airport to avoid taxi queues. The Fado experience is best enjoyed in the evening — confirm reservation in advance as top venues sell out quickly.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel — opt for the full Portuguese breakfast spread with fresh fruit, local cheeses, cured meats, and freshly baked bread.
meals.lunch: Lunch is integrated into the Time Out Market Food Tour — enjoy a curated tasting experience across multiple premium vendors including seafood, petiscos, and Portuguese wines.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Belcanto (2 Michelin stars) in Chiado — Chef José Avillez's flagship restaurant offers a breathtaking tasting menu celebrating reinvented Portuguese classics. Reserve well in advance.

day_by_day.notes: The Time Out Market is busiest on weekends — arriving early in the morning with a guide ensures the best experience before crowds build. The Tile Museum is a 15-minute taxi or Uber ride from the hotel; allocate 2 hours minimum for a thorough visit. Belcanto requires advance reservations — book at least 4–6 weeks ahead.

day_by_day.morning: Belém Historical & Culinary Half-Day — Take a private or guided transfer to the historic riverside district of Belém. Visit the UNESCO-listed Jerónimos Monastery, a breathtaking masterpiece of Manueline Gothic architecture commissioned to celebrate Vasco da Gama's voyage to India. Explore the ornate cloisters and the tombs of Portugal's greatest explorers at a leisurely, unhurried pace.
day_by_day.afternoon: Continue in Belém with a visit to the iconic Tower of Belém standing sentinel on the Tagus River. Walk along the riverside promenade to the Monument to the Discoveries. Stop at the legendary Pastéis de Belém — the original home of the pastel de nata since 1837 — for the definitive custard tart experience sprinkled with cinnamon and powdered sugar. Optionally visit the MAAT (Museum of Art, Architecture and Technology) for a contemporary cultural contrast.
day_by_day.evening: Return to central Lisbon and ascend to the Miradouro de São Pedro de Alcântara viewpoint for golden-hour panoramic views over the city rooftops and the Tagus. Enjoy a glass of vinho verde or a Ginjinha at a nearby terrace bar before dinner.

meals.breakfast: Breakfast at the hotel, followed by a mid-morning coffee and pastel de nata at Pastéis de Belém — a non-negotiable Lisbon ritual.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Solar dos Presuntos or Cervejaria Ramiro (seafood-focused) — alternatively, dine at Feitoria restaurant in Belém, a Michelin-starred waterfront restaurant offering contemporary Portuguese cuisine with Tagus River views.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Alma, Chef Henrique Sá Pessoa's Michelin-starred restaurant in Chiado — celebrating the flavors and ingredients of Portugal's diverse regions in an elegant, intimate setting.

day_by_day.notes: Belém is approximately 6–7 km west of the city center — a scenic 20-minute taxi, Uber, or tram ride (Tram 15E). Sunday mornings can be quieter at the monastery. Wear comfortable shoes for cobblestone walking. The Jerónimos Monastery may have limited access during Sunday morning Mass (typically until 11:00).

day_by_day.morning: Mercado de Campo de Ourique & Local Neighborhood Stroll — Discover one of Lisbon's most beloved and authentically local markets, far from the tourist crowds. Browse stalls of fresh seasonal produce, artisan cheeses, cured meats, freshly baked bread, and regional specialties. Chat with local vendors and gain insight into everyday Lisbon life. Explore the charming Campo de Ourique neighborhood with its tree-lined streets, independent cafés, and Art Nouveau architecture.
day_by_day.afternoon: Guided private history tour of Lisbon's Castelo de São Jorge — the ancient Moorish hilltop castle commanding sweeping 360-degree views over the city, the Tagus, and the Atlantic horizon. Explore the archaeological site revealing layers of Lisbon's history from the Iron Age through Moorish and medieval Portuguese periods. Descend through the Mouraria neighborhood, Lisbon's oldest Muslim quarter, stopping at hidden miradouros and local tile-decorated façades.
day_by_day.evening: Sunset cocktails at a premium rooftop bar such as TOPO Chiado or Sky Bar at Hotel Tivoli Avenida Liberdade, offering spectacular panoramic city views. Follow with a leisurely, indulgent dinner celebrating the best of Portuguese seafood.

meals.breakfast: Light breakfast at the hotel, then supplement with fresh pastries, local cheese, and coffee purchased at Mercado de Campo de Ourique — eat like a true Lisboeta.
meals.lunch: Lunch at Tasca do Chico in Mouraria or Taberna da Rua das Flores in Chiado — both celebrated for honest, ingredient-driven Portuguese cooking in intimate, characterful settings.
meals.dinner: Dinner at Cervejaria Ramiro, Lisbon's legendary seafood institution — indulge in a lavish spread of percebes (barnacles), amêijoas (clams), gambas (prawns), and the famous prego (steak sandwich) to finish.

day_by_day.notes: Campo de Ourique market is liveliest on weekday mornings. The castle is best visited in the afternoon when morning tour groups have cleared. Wear sunscreen and a hat — the castle hilltop is exposed. Book rooftop bar tables in advance for sunset timing, especially in May when evenings are warm and popular.

day_by_day.morning: Spend a final, unhurried morning exploring the elegant Avenida da Liberdade — Lisbon's grand Champs-Élysées-style boulevard lined with luxury boutiques, flagship stores, and Art Deco buildings. Browse Portuguese designer shops and pick up premium souvenirs: fine cork products, vintage azulejo tiles, aged port wine, and artisanal conservas (tinned seafood). Visit the Fundação Calouste Gulbenkian Museum for world-class art collections spanning 4,000 years of civilization.
day_by_day.afternoon: Return to the hotel for a relaxed checkout. Depending on your departure time, enjoy a final pastel de nata and bica (espresso) at a traditional café. Take a private luxury transfer back to the airport with time to spare, reflecting on five extraordinary days in one of Europe's most captivating cities.
day_by_day.evening: Departure from Lisbon — carry the flavors, music, and history of the city with you.

meals.breakfast: A celebratory final breakfast at the hotel — request a special spread of Portuguese specialties including fresh orange juice, local honey, regional cheeses, and warm bread.
meals.lunch: Farewell lunch at Taberna Albricoque or 100 Maneiras — both beloved Lisbon institutions offering creative, produce-driven menus that celebrate Portuguese culinary tradition with a modern twist.
meals.dinner: Airport dinner or in-flight dining — pack a selection of Portuguese snacks from the Avenida da Liberdade gourmet shops: artisan chocolates, tinned sardines, and a bottle of Douro red wine for the journey home.

day_by_day.notes: Confirm hotel checkout time and arrange luggage storage if your flight departs late in the evening. The Gulbenkian Museum is closed on Tuesdays — substitute with the Museu do Design e da Moda (MUDE) or a final walk through Príncipe Real's antique and design shops. Allow at least 2.5–3 hours before your flight for Lisbon Airport check-in and security during peak May travel season.
